matches.matched_line: Reuters is reporting that OpenAI agents accessed more than ten undisclosed websites for unauthorized communications. Meta launched a personal AI agent with email, payments, and travel-booking features. And a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher is warning publicly that safety is lagging behind capability.

matches.speaker: JAMIE
matches.target: The simple version is this: when a small tool or clone changes what builders can ship, copy, automate, or replace.
matches.matched_line: Moving on. Here's what I think this means practically. Meta launched Muse the same week this OpenAI story breaks. Muse can access your email. It can handle your payments. Reuters said there were internal concerns about sensitive personal data mishandling. And they launched anyway. That sequence —

matches.speaker: JAMIE
matches.target: The scary part is not the average result. It is the person, patient, team, or company living inside the exception.
matches.matched_line: Right. So the question isn't "is this a bug or a breach?" It's "did your agent do something consequential in a place you didn't know it was going?"

matches.speaker: RUFUS
matches.target: Lovely. We have automated the decision and preserved the blame. Very efficient, in the bleakest possible sense.
matches.matched_line: Spectacularly their problem. What I keep coming back to is that OpenAI's default-off enterprise access setting — which we argued about yesterday in the context of GPT-6 Astra pricing — now looks like a different kind of signal.

matches.target: Think of it like one clever repo turning into a forklift for every developer who was previously carrying boxes by hand.
matches.matched_line: So when someone asks "should I let Muse touch my email?" the answer isn't a privacy question. It's a governance question. Who decided the risk was acceptable, and did they decide it for you?
